definition: Any process with an uncertain outcome that probability is used to describe, such as rolling a die, sending a packet or picking a random pivot. Each run produces exactly one outcome from the sample space.
example: Rolling two dice is a random experiment with 36 possible ordered outcomes.

definition: The set of every possible outcome of a random experiment, usually written with the Greek capital letter omega. Events are subsets of it, and the whole sample space has probability 1.
example: For one six-sided die the sample space is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.

definition: A single result of a random experiment, one element of the sample space. When every outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is its number of outcomes divided by the total.
example: (1,6) and (6,1) are different outcomes of rolling two dice.

definition: Having the same probability. If a sample space has n equally likely outcomes, each has probability 1/n, and an event's probability is the number of outcomes in it divided by n. Independent uniform choices are each equally likely over their range and unaffected by one another; that is the assumption behind the birthday bound and the analysis of random-pivot quicksort.
example: A fair die's six faces are equally likely, so P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2.

definition: A set of outcomes of a random experiment, that is a subset of the sample space, to which a probability is assigned. The event happens if the actual outcome is one of its members.
example: 'Roll an even number' is the event {2, 4, 6}, with probability 1/2 on a fair die.

definition: A rule that assigns each measurable event a number between zero and one, assigning one to the whole sample space and adding over countably many pairwise disjoint events. In infinite models an event can have probability zero without being impossible, or probability one without containing every outcome.
example: For a fair die, P({6}) = 1/6.

definition: The probability rules requiring nonnegative event probabilities, probability one for the whole sample space, and addition over countably many pairwise disjoint events. Rules such as the complement and inclusion–exclusion identities follow from them.
example: Because the whole sample space has probability one and disjoint probabilities add, an event’s complement has probability one minus that event’s probability.

definition: A subset of the sample space that belongs to the specified collection of events and can therefore be assigned a probability. The collection of all such permitted subsets is the event space; for finite models it can include every subset.

A collection whose members can be listed as a first, second, third and so on, either finitely many or infinitely many (like the whole numbers). Probability's addition axiom is stated for countable collections of disjoint events.
example: The events 'first six on roll 1', 'first six on roll 2', … form a countable collection.

definition: The rule that the probability an event does not happen is 1 minus the probability it does. It makes 'at least one' questions easy: compute the chance of none and subtract from 1.
example: The chance of at least one six in four rolls is 1 − (5/6)⁴ ≈ 0.518.

definition: The probability version of inclusion–exclusion: the chance that A or B happens is P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). The subtraction removes the overlap, which would otherwise be counted twice.
example: With P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.4 and overlap 0.12, P(A or B) = 0.58.

definition: The probability of an event A once you know that another event B has happened, written P(A | B) and read 'A given B'. When P(B) > 0 it equals P(A ∩ B) / P(B): restrict attention to the outcomes in B and ask what fraction are also in A.
example: Given that two dice sum to 8, the chance the first shows 3 is 1/5.

definition: For two events, the probability both happen is the probability of the first multiplied by the conditional probability of the second given the first, provided the first has positive probability. Repeating this rule computes a sequence’s joint probability.
example: Two aces without replacement: 4/52 × 3/51 = 1/221.

definition: For a finite or countable partition into disjoint events covering the sample space, an event’s probability is the sum of its conditional probability within each positive-probability piece multiplied by that piece’s probability. Zero-probability pieces are omitted.
example: 70% of traffic at 1% errors plus 30% at 4% errors gives 1.9% overall.

definition: A set of disjoint events that together cover the whole sample space, so every outcome lies in exactly one of them. The law of total probability adds up over such a partition.
example: 'Request went to region X' and 'request went to region Y' partition all requests when there are only two regions.

definition: Two events are independent when their joint probability equals the product of their separate probabilities. For a collection, mutual independence requires this joint-probability identity for every finite subcollection, which is stronger than independence for every pair.
example: With two fair dice, 'first die even' and 'sum is 7' are independent: 1/12 = 1/2 × 1/6.

definition: Two events or variables are conditionally independent given C when, once you know C, learning one tells you nothing more about the other. Naive Bayes and repeated-test calculations rely on it, and it can fail even when tests look separate.
example: Two medical tests may be independent given illness, but not if both react to the same substance.

definition: The mistaken belief that after a run of one result, the opposite result is 'due'. With independent trials the past has no effect on the next outcome.
example: After five heads in a row, a fair coin still lands heads with probability 1/2.

definition: The fraction of time a component or system is up and able to serve. In series (all parts needed) availabilities multiply; in parallel (any one suffices) the failure probabilities multiply, assuming independent failures.
example: Three services each 99.9% available in series give about 99.7%.

definition: Shorthand for availability written as a run of nines: three nines is 99.9%, six nines is 99.9999%, about 32 seconds of downtime a year.
example: Three independent replicas each down 1% of the time give six nines in the ideal model.

definition: A group of components exposed to a shared cause of failure, such as a rack, power feed or data centre. Separating replicas across failure domains can reduce common infrastructure risks, but does not establish independence or prevent shared software faults.

A cloud-provider deployment area within a region, designed to limit shared infrastructure failures with other zones. Provider terminology and physical arrangements vary; a fault confined to one zone can be tolerated only by systems with sufficient replicas and working failover.
example: Replicas across zones can tolerate a zone outage when a sufficient quorum remains reachable and failover works.

definition: Failures that are statistically associated rather than independent, often because of a shared cause such as power loss or a bad deployment. Positive association between a pair makes their joint failure more likely than multiplying their marginal probabilities predicts; general multi-component dependence needs its own joint model.
example: Three replicas in one rack can all fail in one power cut.

definition: A failure in which one component going down shifts load onto others, making them more likely to fail too. It makes later failures more likely given earlier ones, so failures are not independent.

Estimating a model probability or expectation by repeatedly sampling the random model. For independent identically distributed runs with finite variance, the standard error shrinks in proportion to the reciprocal square root of the run count; this does not validate the model against reality.
example: A million simulated sets of four rolls give a fraction close to 0.518.

definition: A random experiment with two labelled outcomes, success and failure. Independent repetitions with one common success probability underlie the binomial and geometric distributions; a single Bernoulli trial does not itself assert independence from other trials.
example: Each packet sent over a link that drops 1% of packets is a Bernoulli trial with p = 0.01 for 'lost'.

definition: The standard deviation of an estimator across repeated samples, in the estimator’s units. For the mean of independent identically distributed observations with finite variance, it is the observation standard deviation divided by the square root of the positive sample size; bias is a separate source of estimation error.
example: 400 requests with standard deviation 80 ms give a standard error of 4 ms.

definition: In Bayesian reasoning, a possible explanation or state of the world whose probability you want, such as 'this payment is fraud'. Evidence updates its probability.
The probability of a hypothesis before seeing the current evidence, often the base rate. In Bayes' theorem it is multiplied by the likelihood and divided by the evidence term.
example: If 1 in 1,000 payments is fraud, the prior probability of fraud is 0.001.

definition: In Bayes' theorem, P(E | H): how probable the observed evidence is if the hypothesis is true. Note it is a probability of the evidence, not of the hypothesis.
example: A test that catches 99% of cases has likelihood 0.99 for a positive result given illness.

definition: In Bayes' theorem, P(E): the overall probability of the observed evidence, from every possible cause. It is found with the law of total probability and makes the posteriors add up to 1.
example: With 1% prevalence, 99% sensitivity and 5% false positives, the evidence term P(positive) is 0.0594.

definition: The probability of a hypothesis after taking the evidence into account, P(H | E). Yesterday's posterior becomes today's prior when more evidence arrives.
example: After one positive test in the 1%/99%/5% example, the posterior is about 1/6.

definition: How common something is in the population before any test or evidence, for example the fraction of payments that are fraud. It is usually the prior in Bayes' theorem.
example: A condition affecting 1% of people has a base rate of 0.01.

definition: The mistake of judging P(cause | evidence) mainly from P(evidence | cause) while ignoring how rare the cause is. With rare events, even a small false positive rate can make most alerts false.
example: A fraud model that catches 98% of fraud and flags 1% of legitimate payments flags 10,970 of a million payments, but only 980 are fraud.

definition: The fraction of real positive cases that a test or detector correctly flags, P(positive result | real case). Called sensitivity in medicine and recall in machine learning.
example: A test that detects 99 of 100 ill people has sensitivity 99%.

definition: The fraction of real negative cases that a test correctly reports as negative, P(negative | not a case). It equals 1 minus the false positive rate.
example: A 5% false positive rate means 95% specificity.

definition: A result that says 'yes' (alert, positive test, significant) when the true answer is 'no'. In hypothesis testing it is a Type I error.
example: A healthy person testing positive is a false positive.

definition: A result that says 'no' when the true answer is 'yes', such as a test missing a real case. In hypothesis testing it is a Type II error.
A real case that a test or detector correctly flags as positive. Precision is true positives divided by all positives flagged.
example: 99 ill people who test positive are 99 true positives.

definition: The fraction of real negatives that are wrongly flagged as positive, P(positive | not a case). It equals 1 minus the specificity; for a Bloom filter it is the chance an absent key looks present.
example: A test that flags 5 of every 100 healthy people has a 5% false positive rate.

definition: In classification, the proportion of predicted positives that are actually positive, when positive predictions have nonzero probability. It depends on prevalence as well as sensitivity and false-positive rate. With positive sensitivity and positive false-positive rate fixed, lowering prevalence lowers precision; zero false positives are an important exception.
example: 980 real frauds among 10,970 alerts is a precision of about 8.9%.

definition: A way of expressing probability as the chance of yes divided by the chance of no, written as a ratio such as 1 : 99. Odds of O correspond to a probability of O / (1 + O).
example: A probability of 1% is odds of 1 : 99; odds of 1 : 5 are a probability of 1/6.

definition: The probability of the observed evidence under one hypothesis divided by its probability under the alternative, when the latter probability is positive. Multiplying prior odds by this ratio gives posterior odds in a binary model with positive priors.
example: A test with 99% sensitivity and 5% false positives has likelihood ratio 19.8.

definition: Revising the probability of a hypothesis with Bayes' theorem as each piece of evidence arrives, so that each posterior becomes the next prior.
example: Two independent positive tests take odds of 1 : 99 to about 4 : 1.

definition: A classifier using Bayes’ theorem with a model in which features are conditionally independent given the class. This makes class scores products of feature likelihoods; useful classification does not guarantee that the resulting probabilities are well calibrated.
example: A spam filter multiplies P(spam) by the chance of each word in spam, and does the same for ham.

definition: Software that classifies email as spam (unwanted bulk mail) or ham (legitimate mail). Bayesian spam filters, popularised by Paul Graham's 2002 essay 'A Plan for Spam', score emails from word statistics.
The usual name in spam filtering for legitimate, wanted email: the opposite of spam. A spam filter learns word statistics separately for spam and for ham.
example: If 40% of email is spam, the other 60% is ham.

definition: Additive smoothing adds a positive pseudo-count to each category in a fixed finite vocabulary, then normalises by the total adjusted count. Laplace or add-one smoothing uses a pseudo-count of one, so the denominator is the original total plus the vocabulary size; categories outside the vocabulary need a separate policy.
example: A word seen 0 times in 50,000 spam words with a 10,000-word vocabulary gets 1/60,000 instead of 0.

definition: When a floating-point result is too close to zero to be represented at normal precision, it can become subnormal or round to zero. Sufficiently long products of small probabilities can do this; summing their finite logarithms avoids product underflow.
example: Multiplying 400 probabilities of 0.01 gives 10⁻⁸⁰⁰, far below the smallest double, about 5 × 10⁻³²⁴.

definition: The fixed set of distinct tokens (words) a text classifier knows about. Smoothing gives every token in it a non-zero probability; tokens outside it need a separate policy.

Confusing the chance of the evidence given innocence with the chance of innocence given the evidence. A 1-in-a-million match probability does not mean a 1-in-a-million chance of innocence, because many innocent people could match.

Software that examines network traffic or host activity for signs of attack and raises alerts. Alert precision depends on attack prevalence and the detector’s sensitivity and false positive rate; rarity alone does not determine it.
Building programs that learn patterns from example data rather than following hand-written rules, for example a classifier trained on labelled emails.
A program or model that assigns each input to one of several classes, such as spam or ham, fraud or legitimate.
A data set where one class is far rarer than another, such as 0.1% fraud. Accuracy becomes misleading: always predicting the common class scores 99.9%.
The fraction of all predictions a classifier gets right. On imbalanced data it can be very high for a useless model, so precision and recall are reported instead.
Google's discipline of running production systems with software engineering methods; its book advises alerting on user-visible symptoms rather than noisy internal causes.

A test that can pass or fail on unchanged code and relevant inputs because of uncontrolled scheduling, random choices or unstable conditions. Flaky failures can obscure genuine regressions; the proportion of false alarms also depends on how often real defects occur.

A measurable numerical function of the outcome of a random experiment. Its rule is fixed while its realised value depends on the uncertain outcome; the distribution describes how likely its possible values are.
example: X = the sum of two dice maps the outcome (3, 5) to 8.

definition: The probability law describing a random variable’s values. A discrete law can be described by probabilities of individual values; a continuous law with a density gives interval probabilities by areas under that density. Some laws are mixed or have no density.
For a discrete random variable, the function giving the probability of each exact value, P(X = x). Its values add up to 1.
example: For the sum of two dice the PMF at 8 is 5/36.

definition: For a probability law that admits a density, a nonnegative function whose area over an interval gives the probability of that interval. Density heights are not point probabilities and can exceed one.
The function giving the probability that a random variable is at most a value, P(X ≤ x). The standard normal CDF is written Φ (capital phi).
example: Φ(1.96) ≈ 0.975 for the standard normal.

definition: One minus the CDF, P(X > x): the probability of exceeding a value. Libraries such as scipy.stats compute it directly to keep small tail probabilities accurate.

The probability-weighted average of a random variable’s values when that expectation exists. For independent identically distributed repetitions with finite absolute expectation, sample means converge to it; it need not be a possible observed value.
example: One fair die has expected value 3.5.

definition: For independent identically distributed observations with finite absolute expectation, sample averages converge to that expectation as the sample grows. In particular, the chance of exceeding any fixed positive estimation error tends to zero; this does not mean the error decreases on every new observation.
example: A million die rolls average very close to 3.5.

definition: The distribution of the number of independent trials, each with the same positive success probability, up to and including the first success. Its mean is the reciprocal of that probability; after any possible run of failures, the remaining wait has the same distribution.
example: A retry that succeeds 20% of the time takes 5 attempts on average.

definition: For a variable with finite second moment, a measure of spread: the average squared distance of a random variable from its mean, E[(X − μ)²], which also equals E[X²] − (E[X])². Its square root is the standard deviation.
example: One fair die roll has variance 35/12 ≈ 2.92.

definition: The square root of the variance, written σ (sigma): a typical distance of values from their mean, in the same units as the data.
example: One die roll has standard deviation about 1.71.

definition: The expected square of a random variable. A finite second moment ensures a finite mean and finite variance; some variables instead have infinite second moment and no finite variance.

The rule that the expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values, E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], and E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b, for finite absolute expectations, even when the variables are dependent. It turns hard counting problems into sums of simple probabilities.
example: 100 people each with a 1/100 chance of their own hat gives 1 expected match.

definition: For random variables with finite second moments, a measure of how they move together: E[XY] − E[X]E[Y]. Positive means they tend to rise together; zero means uncorrelated.
Two random variables with finite second moments are uncorrelated when their covariance is zero. Independence implies this condition, but zero covariance does not generally imply independence.
A random variable that is 1 if a given event happens and 0 otherwise. Its expected value equals the event's probability, so counts written as sums of indicators have easy expectations by linearity.
example: One indicator per person for 'got their own hat' sums to the number of matches.

definition: A load-balancing technique: pick two servers at random and send the job to the less loaded one. In the balanced-allocations model it shrinks the maximum load dramatically compared with one random choice.

A pair of array positions where the earlier value is larger than the later one. Adjacent-swap insertion sort uses one swap per inversion; the usual shifting version uses one rightward shift per inversion. For a uniformly random permutation of distinct values, each pair is inverted with probability one-half.
example: [3, 1, 2] has two inversions: (3,1) and (3,2).

definition: The constant γ ≈ 0.5772, the limit of the gap between the harmonic number H_n and ln(n). It explains the '+ 0.577' in H_n ≈ ln(n) + 0.577.
How many independent uniformly random draws with replacement it takes to see every one of n types one or more times. The expected number is n × H_n, about n ln n.
example: Hitting all 50 shards takes about 225 random requests on average.

definition: For a non-negative random variable and any a > 0, P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X] / a. It bounds the tail using only the mean.
example: With mean latency 20 ms, at most 20% of requests can take 100 ms or more.

definition: For a random variable with mean μ and finite standard deviation σ > 0, P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k² for any k > 0. It bounds two-sided deviations using the variance.
example: At most 1/9 of any such distribution lies 3 or more standard deviations from its mean.

definition: A part of a distribution far from its centre, used to discuss extreme outcomes and their probabilities. A tail bound limits such probabilities; this alone does not classify the tail as heavy or light.

For a convex function, the function of an expected value is no larger than the expected function value, when the variable lies in the function’s domain and the relevant expectations exist. For positive transfer speeds, taking reciprocals explains why averaging speeds can underestimate average duration.
A function whose coordinate plot curves upwards, so any line segment joining two plotted points lies on or above the plot, like x² or 1/x for positive x.

The distribution of a success count in a fixed nonnegative number of independent trials with one common success probability between zero and one. Its mean is the trial count times that probability, and its variance is that mean times the failure probability.
example: Packets lost out of 100 at a 1% loss rate are binomial with n = 100, p = 0.01.

definition: A distribution on nonnegative integer counts with a nonnegative expected-count parameter; its mean and variance both equal that parameter. Counts in intervals of specified duration in a homogeneous Poisson process have this law, and suitable independent rare-trial counts can be approximated by it.
example: A Poisson count with mean 5 exceeds 9 with probability about 3.2%.

definition: A model of events arriving at random times with a constant average rate and independent counts in non-overlapping intervals. Its counts per window are Poisson and its gaps have an exponential distribution.
The fact that independent Poisson counts (or processes) add to another Poisson count whose mean is the sum of the means.
example: Independent streams with means 2 and 3 merge into a Poisson count with mean 5.

definition: Keeping each event of a Poisson process independently with probability q gives another Poisson process with mean scaled by q.
example: If 2% of 5 requests per second are errors, errors are Poisson with 0.1 per second.

definition: The gap between one event and the next in an arrival process. In a Poisson process with rate r the gaps are exponential with mean 1/r.
A continuous distribution of waiting times with constant hazard: the time until the next event of a Poisson process. It is memoryless, the continuous cousin of the geometric distribution.

A waiting-time law is memoryless when, conditional on still waiting after a possible elapsed period, the remaining wait has the original distribution. The standard proper nondegenerate memoryless laws are geometric on positive integers and exponential on nonnegative real time.
When count data have a variance clearly larger than their mean, so a single Poisson model (where mean equals variance) does not fit. Bursts and mixed populations are common causes.

A symmetric bell-shaped continuous distribution specified by its mean and positive standard deviation. About 68%, 95% and 99.7% lies within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean; these are two-sided bands, not one-sided percentile labels.
The normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Any observation from another normal distribution converts to this scale through its z-score.
example: A standard normal exceeds 1.96 about 2.5% of the time.

definition: For a normal distribution, about 68.3% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, 95.4% within two and 99.7% within three.
How many standard deviations a value lies from the mean: z = (x − μ) / σ. Used to read normal probabilities and as the test statistic in z-tests.
example: With mean 100 and standard deviation 10, the value 120 has z = 2.

definition: The theorem that the suitably centred and scaled sum (or mean) of many independent, identically distributed variables with finite non-zero variance approaches a normal distribution as the sample grows.
example: The sum of 100 dice is close to normal with mean 350 and standard deviation about 17.1.

definition: When approximating a whole-number count with a continuous normal distribution, treating the value k as the interval from k − 0.5 to k + 0.5 to improve accuracy.
Describes a collection of observations that are mutually independent and all have the same distribution. Merely sharing the same distribution does not imply independence.

A scientific computing library for Python, built on NumPy. Its statistics module provides distribution objects: discrete laws have probability mass methods, continuous laws have density methods, and both offer cumulative and survival probabilities.
When data packets sent across a network fail to arrive, for example because a queue filled up or a link was noisy. TCP detects losses and retransmits.
Sending a packet again after it was lost or not acknowledged in time; the mechanism TCP uses to deliver data reliably over a network that can lose packets.

A set containing more than half of a fixed voting membership. A five-member system requires three reachable cooperating members for a majority; node availability alone does not guarantee that the protocol or service is functioning.
The process by which nodes in a cluster choose one node to coordinate, for example after the old leader fails. During an election the cluster may briefly be unable to accept writes.
A network failure that splits a cluster into groups of nodes that can no longer talk to each other, even though each node is still running.
Estimating how much hardware or how many workers a service needs to handle its load with acceptable risk of overload, often from arrival-count distributions.
Traffic that follows a daily rhythm, high during the day and low at night. It breaks the constant-rate assumption of a simple Poisson model.
Waiting progressively longer between retries of a failed request, so that an overloaded service is not hammered harder. A retry storm is the opposite: many clients retrying at once and adding load.
The sum of the values divided by how many there are, written x̄ for a sample. It is pulled strongly by outliers and is what matters for totals such as resource use.
example: 99 requests at 10 ms and one at 5,000 ms have mean 59.9 ms.

definition: The middle value when the data are sorted (for an even count, conventionally the average of the two middle values). It describes the typical case and is robust to outliers.
example: The median of 99 × 10 ms and one 5,000 ms is 10 ms.

definition: An observation far from most of the others, such as one timeout among fast requests. Extreme observations can strongly influence the mean; the median is more resistant because it depends on central ranks rather than the magnitudes of tail observations.
A distribution that is lopsided rather than symmetric; a right-skewed shape extends farther towards larger values, as latency often does.

A threshold defined by a chosen quantile convention. Under empirical nearest rank, at least the requested percentage of observations are at or below the threshold, allowing ties; the population 50th percentile is a median, while sample conventions can differ.
example: A p99 latency of 420 ms means at least 99% of requests took 420 ms or less.

definition: A general cut point of a distribution expressed as a fraction from 0 to 1; percentiles are quantiles in per cent.

A sample percentile convention: for a nonempty sorted sample and a requested percentage greater than zero through 100, choose the observation at the rounded-up percentage rank. Returning the minimum at zero is a separate extension.
example: The nearest-rank p90 of 10 values is the 9th smallest.

definition: A summary of data as counts in fixed value ranges (buckets). Histograms with the same buckets merge by adding counts, so fleet-wide percentiles can be estimated from them.

A compact data structure that summarises observations to estimate quantiles such as percentiles. Some sketches support merging compatible summaries across servers; t-digest is a widely used mergeable example.
A high-dynamic-range histogram library for recording latencies with bounded relative error, widely used for tail-latency measurement.
An open-source monitoring system and time-series database; its histogram metrics store bucket counts that can be summed across servers to estimate percentiles.

One request triggers requests to multiple backends. In a design that waits for all those results, the slowest required backend determines that part of the response time; other designs can return after a quorum or first acceptable result.
A 2013 Communications of the ACM paper by Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso on why rare backend slowness becomes common user slowness in fan-out systems, and on mitigations such as hedged requests.
Sending a backup copy of a slow request to another replica after a short delay and using whichever answer arrives first, to cut tail latency at the cost of some extra load.

The number of observations in a sample. For iid finite-variance means, standard error decreases with its square root; ordinary fixed-sample A/B tests choose it in advance, while valid sequential designs use their own stopping rules.

A range computed from data by a procedure that, over many repeated experiments, contains the true value a stated fraction of the time (for example 95%). It is not a 95% probability statement about one particular interval.
example: Mean 250 ms with standard error 4 ms gives a 95% interval of about 242 to 258 ms.

definition: The simple confidence interval for a proportion, p̂ ± 1.96 × √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n). It is inaccurate near 0 or 1 or with few successes or failures.

A confidence-interval procedure for a binomial proportion obtained by inverting a score test. It often has better coverage than the simple Wald interval near zero or one or with small samples; it is distinct from an exact binomial interval.

Student’s t-distribution is a symmetric probability law indexed by degrees of freedom, with heavier tails than a standard normal. A Student-t interval for a mean accounts for estimating the standard deviation and has exact stated coverage for normal iid samples of at least two observations; it approaches the normal interval for large samples.
In Bayesian statistics, an interval that contains the unknown value with a stated posterior probability, given the prior and the model.

Statistical correlation between observations of the same process at different time lags. Positive serial correlation can make an independence-based standard error too small; negative correlation or a different correlation pattern can have a different effect.
Another workload on the same shared machine or cloud host that competes for CPU, cache, disk or network and makes your measurements vary.
Slower early runs of a benchmark while caches fill, code is compiled or connections are opened, which bias results if not discarded or balanced.
An experiment that randomly splits users between a control (A) and a variant (B) and compares a metric. Random assignment balances other factors between the groups in expectation.
In an A/B test, the control is the group that keeps the current version and the variant (treatment) gets the change; each group is called an arm.
The default assumption a statistical test tries to find evidence against, usually that there is no effect. Written H₀ ('H-nought').
The hypothesis of a real effect, often of a stated size, against which the null is tested; power is computed under it.
A number computed from the data that measures how far the result is from what the null hypothesis predicts, often in standard errors, such as a z statistic.
The probability, assuming the null hypothesis and the sampling model, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
example: A z of 2.31 gives a two-sided p-value of about 0.021.

definition: A result is statistically significant when its p-value is below a threshold fixed in advance, the significance level α, commonly 0.05.

Rejecting a true null hypothesis: a false positive. A test designed at a stated significance level aims to bound this probability under its specified model; the actual rate can be smaller, or differ when an approximation is inaccurate.
Failing to reject the null hypothesis when a real effect exists: a false negative. Its rate is β, and power is 1 − β.
The probability that a test detects a real effect of a stated size, 1 − β. Designs commonly aim for 80%; too few users makes a test underpowered.

A statistical hypothesis test that compares a suitably standardised statistic with the standard normal distribution. A two-proportion z-test uses a pooled rate under the equal-rate null and needs sufficiently large independent counts for its normal approximation.
example: 10.0% versus 11.0% on 10,000 users each gives z ≈ 2.31.

definition: The overall rate from combining both arms of a test, used to estimate the standard error under the null hypothesis that both arms share one rate.
example: 1,000 + 1,100 conversions out of 20,000 users is a pooled rate of 0.105.

definition: The magnitude of a difference, expressed in stated units such as percentage points or relative lift. Practical importance also depends on context; approximate sample requirements for a fixed-power comparison often scale with the reciprocal square of the target effect.
The unit for the simple difference between two percentages: 10% to 11% is a rise of 1 percentage point, which is a 10% relative increase.
The fraction of users who complete a target action, such as buying or signing up; a common A/B test metric.

Inspecting an ordinary fixed-sample test repeatedly and choosing to stop when it becomes significant. Such stopping can inflate its false positive probability; the amount depends on the test and look schedule, and valid sequential methods account for stopping.
Statistical methods designed for looking at results repeatedly while data arrive, with error rates controlled across all the looks.

Testing a family of hypotheses creates opportunities for false rejections. The chance of at least one false rejection depends on the number, dependence and error probabilities of the tests; family-wise or false-discovery procedures control specified error measures.
example: 20 independent tests at 0.05 give a 64% chance of a false win.

definition: Testing each of k hypotheses at α / k so that the chance of any false positive across the family stays at most α, without needing independence.
example: 20 metrics at α = 0.05 need p < 0.0025 each.

definition: The probability of at least one false positive among a whole family of tests.

The expected proportion of rejected hypotheses whose null hypotheses are actually true, counting the proportion as zero when there are no rejections. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure controls this measure under independence or suitable positive dependence.

An outcome measure selected before an experiment as the main basis for its decision. Declaring one limits opportunities to choose a favourable result afterwards; additional claims and exploratory metrics still need appropriate interpretation or control for multiple comparisons.

An observed allocation imbalance that is unusually large under the planned assignment model. It is evidence to investigate assignment, eligibility or logging; it is not logical proof of a specific defect.
example: 503,000 versus 497,000 on a planned 50/50 split is 6 standard deviations off.

definition: A family of statistical tests comparing observed and model-expected counts. An allocation check can detect a mismatch that would be unlikely under the planned random split; it cannot establish that chance is impossible.
A temporary change in behaviour because something is new (novelty) or while users adapt to it (learning), which can make short A/B tests misleading.
When a trend that appears in every subgroup reverses or disappears once the groups are combined, because the groups are mixed in different proportions.
Whether an effect is large enough to matter in practice, as opposed to merely being statistically detectable.
A comparison of groups that were not randomly assigned, such as users who chose to enable a feature; differences may come from who chose, not the feature.
The number of stored keys divided by the number of buckets or slots in a hash table, written α. Expected lookup cost depends on it, so tables resize to keep it bounded.
example: 2,000 keys in 1,000 buckets is a load factor of 2.

definition: The modelling assumption that each key is hashed independently to a uniformly random bucket. Real hash functions only approximate it, and attackers can break it.
A hash-table collision strategy in which each bucket holds a list of all keys that hashed there; a lookup scans one bucket's list.
A hash-table collision strategy that stores every key in the array itself and probes other slots when the home slot is taken. It slows sharply as the load factor approaches 1.
An open-addressing scheme that, on a collision, tries the next slot, then the next, until it finds a free one or the key.
example: At load factor 0.9 an unsuccessful search averages about 50 probes.

definition: Unordered pairs of distinct items assigned the same value or bucket. With independent uniform assignments, the expected count is the number of pairs divided by the number of possible values; it differs from both the number of occupied buckets and the number of insertions that encounter a used bucket.
example: 1,000 keys in 1,000 buckets give about 500 colliding pairs.

definition: A denial-of-service attack that sends many keys crafted to collide in a server's hash tables, turning cheap inserts into linear-time scans. Demonstrated against many web frameworks in 2011.
An attack that prevents legitimate users from using a service by exhausting its resources, such as CPU spent on colliding hash-table inserts.
An HTTP request that sends data, such as form fields, to a server; its parameter names are often stored in a hash table.
A server-side web programming language. After the 2011 hash-flooding disclosures it added the max_input_vars setting to cap the number of request parameters.

A hash function that takes a key as well as the input. An appropriately designed function with an unpredictable secret key makes precomputed collision attacks harder; resistance depends on the function, key handling and attacker’s capabilities.
A fast keyed hash function designed in 2012 by Aumasson and Bernstein for hash tables; CPython and Rust use variants of it to resist hash flooding.

Choosing a random secret seed for string hashing when a process starts, so collision patterns differ between runs; enabled by default in Python 3.3 and later. Python configuration can disable this randomisation; not every key type uses a randomised hash.
The standard, reference implementation of the Python language, written in C.
Java's standard hash table class. Its default load factor is 0.75, and when one bucket grows large it can convert that bucket into a balanced tree (treeification).

A 128-bit identifier format specified by RFC 9562. Version 4 contains 122 random bits plus fixed version and variant bits; independent well-generated values have a collision risk determined by the number issued, rather than an absolute uniqueness guarantee.

The distributed version-control system. It names objects by hash and shows short hexadecimal abbreviations, lengthening them automatically as a repository grows until each abbreviation names just one object.
Base-16 notation using the digits 0–9 and a–f; each hex character encodes 4 bits.
example: Seven hex characters encode 28 bits.

definition: A 128-bit cryptographic hash function from 1992 that is now broken: practical collisions have been found far faster than the generic birthday bound.
A 160-bit cryptographic hash function from 1995; a practical collision was published in 2017 (SHAttered), so it is deprecated for security.
A hash function designed so that finding collisions, or an input with a given output, is infeasible. An ideal b-bit one resists generic collision search for about 2^(b/2) work.
Finding a collision in a hash function by hashing many random inputs and waiting for two to match, which takes about the square root of the number of possible outputs.
example: A 128-bit hash falls to about 2⁶⁴ evaluations.

definition: Finding an input that hashes to one specific given output. For an ideal b-bit hash it needs about 2^b work, far more than finding any collision.
How hard it is to find any two inputs with the same hash; for an ideal b-bit hash it is about b/2 bits because of the birthday bound.

An element chosen to partition a quicksort subarray. For distinct keys, fresh independent uniform pivots with the stated partition comparison model give expected input-length-times-logarithm comparisons for each fixed input.
A quicksort-like algorithm that finds an element at a specified sorted rank by recursing into only one side of each partition; with random pivots it runs in expected linear time.
A hybrid sort used by many C++ std::sort implementations: quicksort that switches to heapsort if recursion gets too deep, guaranteeing O(n log n) worst case.
A comparison sort that builds a binary heap and repeatedly removes the largest element; always O(n log n).
A quicksort variant by Orson Peters that detects bad patterns and falls back to heapsort; Go's sort package adopted it in Go 1.19.
The unstable sort used in current versions of Rust's standard library, by Lukas Bergdoll and Orson Peters, which combines quicksort's fast average case with heapsort's fast worst case.
A sort that keeps equal elements in their original relative order; Python's list sort and Java's object-array sort are stable.

A deterministic algorithm that produces numbers that look random from a seed. Python's random module is fine for simulations and pivots but predictable, so security tokens should use the secrets module.
Python's standard-library module for generating cryptographically strong random numbers, suitable for passwords and tokens.
An embedded key-value storage engine from Meta, built on a log-structured merge tree; it can keep a Bloom filter per file to skip files that cannot contain a key.
The part of a database that manages how records are stored and retrieved, including in-memory structures, caches and persistent storage where used.

Input/output: exchanging data with a device, storage system or network. Its cost depends on the device, access pattern and cache state; avoiding unnecessary physical reads can reduce storage-query latency.

A Bloom filter’s false positive rate is the chance that an absent key’s selected bits are all set, so the filter reports possible membership. Bits per key means filter bits divided by inserted distinct-key count and controls the memory/error trade-off; under the usual large-filter ideal hashing approximation, ten bits per key and seven hash functions give about 0.82%.
A guarantee that holds with probability tending to 1 as the input size grows, often at least 1 − 1/n.

An adversary that can choose later actions based on observations of earlier execution. This is more powerful than choosing one bad input in advance; randomised guarantees must specify which adversarial model they cover.
An algorithm that decides whether a number is prime; Miller–Rabin is a fast randomised one that may wrongly call a composite 'probably prime' with small probability.
One thousandth of a second, the usual unit for request latency.
example: A 100 ms request takes a tenth of a second.

definition: One million bytes (10⁶). MB/s, megabytes per second, measures transfer speed.
example: A 100 MB file at 10 MB/s takes 10 s.

definition: One thousand bytes (10³) in SI usage; some software uses KB for 1,024 bytes, which is properly a kibibyte (KiB).

Components arranged so that every one must work for the whole system to work, like services a request passes through one after another. With independent failures, the system's availability is the product of the components' availabilities.
example: Three 99.9% services in series give about 99.7%.

definition: Components arranged so that any one working is enough, like replicas behind perfect failover. With independent failures, the system fails only if all fail, so the failure probabilities multiply.
example: Three replicas each down 1% of the time are all down 0.01³ = one millionth of the time.

definition: A random variable measuring how long (in trials or in time) you wait until an event happens, such as the first success. Geometric and exponential distributions are the standard waiting-time models.

A function that does not just scale and shift its input, such as x² or 1/x. For such functions the expected value of f(X) is generally not f of the expected value, which is why averaging speeds misleads about average times.
example: Speeds of 10 and 90 MB/s average 50 MB/s, but 100 MB takes 5.6 s on average, not 2 s.

definition: A distribution whose upper-tail probabilities cannot be bounded, for every chosen positive decay rate, by a constant multiple of the corresponding decaying natural exponential across all sufficiently large thresholds. Bounded and exponential distributions can be right-skewed while remaining light-tailed, so right skew alone does not establish a heavy tail.

A statistical association in which two quantities tend to be above their means together, giving positive covariance when finite second moments exist. It does not mean every pair of observations moves in the same direction.
A fraction of a population or sample possessing a specified property, between zero and one. A sample proportion estimates a population probability under a specified sampling model.
The natural logarithm of a positive probability score. Because the logarithm is strictly increasing, maximising a positive score and maximising its log give the same mathematical class choice.
A collection of observations used to learn about a population or process. Its selection method, dependence and representativeness affect what can be inferred from it.

An interval obtained by inverting binomial tail probabilities rather than using a normal approximation. The usual equal-tailed Clopper–Pearson procedure has coverage at least the requested confidence level, and can be conservative because counts are discrete.
An unwanted change in one stored or transmitted binary digit. Such an error may be detected or corrected by an error-control scheme; it is not necessarily silent data corruption.

Methods for summarising observations and learning about a population or process from data. Inference combines the observations with assumptions about sampling and a model, so conclusions depend on those assumptions.

The specified collection of measurable subsets of a sample space to which probability is assigned. It contains the whole space and is closed under complements and countable unions; in a finite model it can contain every subset.

The function that raises Euler’s number, about 2.718, to a real-valued power. It is the inverse of the natural logarithm and turns sums in its exponent into products; probability models use it in Poisson laws and birthday approximations.

A procedure that uses sample data and a specified sampling model to assess evidence against a null hypothesis. Its rejection rule and assumptions determine its Type I error probability; failure to reject does not prove the null is true.
